headline: The 4-day week will be accepted by IT workers but rejected as irrelevant or exploitative by the broader urban workforce, creating a two-tier adoption split along income lines.
say_do_gap: People say they're skeptical (41% support) but 53% would adopt it, revealing a 'complain but comply' dynamic driven by the extra day off outweighing 10-hour day dread.
summary: High-income IT employees (₹75k+) embrace the policy (net +0.77, 67-72% adoption) for the three-day weekend, while low-income workers (<₹35k) resist (net -0.43, 16-45% adoption) seeing 10-hour days as unpaid overtime. The policy passes because the target IT cohort drives adoption, but it deepens inequality perception.

drivers.explanation: 35% cite extra leisure; adoption jumps to 56-59% for 18-44 age groups who value recovery time.
30% flag salary stagnation; <₹15k segment adopts at only 16% (net -0.58), ₹15-35k at 45% (net -0.28).
20% see corporate hype; women net 0.00 (adopt 49%) vs men +0.31 (adopt 56%), suggesting trust gap.
₹75k-2L net +0.76 (adopt 67%), >₹2L net +0.78 (adopt 72%) — the actual IT workforce skews strongly positive.

segments_at_risk.why: Net -0.58, 16% adoption — view 10-hour days as survival threat, not perk; no IT relevance.
Net -0.28, 45% adoption — include gig/blue-collar who can't compress hours; see policy as elite capture.
Net -0.59, 41% adoption — health/stamina concerns make 10-hour days infeasible; fixed-income anxiety.
Net -0.05, 36% adoption — lowest regional adoption; possible sector mix or cultural resistance to long days.

surprise: Adoption intent (53%) exceeds declared support (41%) by 12 points — the 'Netflix quote' factor: people publicly critique but privately want the third day off.
fix: Add a mandatory 'no productivity penalty' clause: same output expectations, explicit opt-out to 5×8 with no career impact, and overtime pay trigger at 44 weekly hours.
rewrite: India's largest IT-services firms jointly announce a 4-day, 40-hour work week (10 hours/day) for all employees from next quarter, with no salary change. Crucially, performance targets stay at 5-day levels — no crunch — and any employee may revert to 5×8 without career penalty. Hours beyond 44/week trigger overtime pay.
watch_outs: Low-income backlash fuels 'IT privilege' narrative — expect political pressure to extend policy to non-IT sectors where 10-hour days are unsafe.
Women's neutral stance (net 0.00) signals caregiving load makes 10-hour days harder; monitor attrition.
East region's 36% adoption may reflect non-IT industrial base — pilot there first.
Q4 FY26 earnings (April 9) will be scrutinized for productivity drops; any miss kills credibility.
